text: Error 1205 tells the victim's session what happened. It doesn't tell YOU, the developer trying to prevent the next one, the full picture. For that, SQL Server can capture a deadlock graph.
A deadlock graph is an XML capture of exactly what you'd want to know: which two processes were involved, what resources each one held and was waiting for, and which one was chosen as the victim.

The modern, documented way to capture one is Extended Events, subscribed to the xml_deadlock_report event. Start a session for it, and the next time the deadlock monitor resolves a deadlock, the full graph is captured — viewable right in SSMS's Extended Events UI, which can even render it as an actual graphical diagram.

There's an older method you'll still encounter: trace flag 1222, enabled with DBCC TRACEON, which writes deadlock information to the SQL Server error log, or capturing it through SQL Server Profiler. Both still work, but Extended Events is the current recommended approach.

Whichever way it's captured, the graph shows two or more process nodes — session ID, the statement running, the isolation level — plus resource nodes showing what each process held and what it was waiting for. That's the same held-and-wants cycle from last lesson, now with real object names and real session IDs. One process node is explicitly marked as the victim.
Next up: the last piece of this lock cluster — real, standard advice for actually preventing deadlocks in the first place, and handling the ones that still happen.
